MetaCheck Report

Stress Generation Across Hours, Days, and 1 Month

2026-11-14 · Metacheck 0.4.4.1 · DOI 10.1177/21677026261471782

3to fix3to check0to decide by hand2fine7not applicable

To fix (3)

To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 1 potential power analysis.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3.5:4b’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: sample_size, alpha_level, effect_size, effect_size_metric, software

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
posthoc other NA NA 0.8 NA NA NA

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as ‘post-hoc’. Calculating observed power is almost never useful. If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

text
Participants were primarily German (55%) or Swiss (27%). More details on the sample can be found in Section 1 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f. Power simulations indicated that we had sufficient power (1 -β ≥ .80) to identify small stress generation effects across all three timescales (hours: β = 0.05; days: β = 0.12; weeks: β = 0.08) and medium-sized interaction effects across timescales (β = 0.23).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 103 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 124 of 194 data columns (64%) are documented in a codebook; 70 are not.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 2 codebook/README/label sources and 194 data columns across 4 files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 2 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 4 distinct packages/libraries: careless, psych, readxl, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 2 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 2 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

1 of 2 scripts ran to the end: 1 stopped with an error.

Script Result What happened
01 Data Preparation Extern.R Ran to the end
Supplement_SG_v2.R Stopped with an error Error in kable_styling(., bootstrap_options = c(“striped”, “hover”, “condensed”), : could not find function “kable_styling”

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • Supplement_SG_v2.R: kable_styling

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

Other problems in the files

  • 01 Data Preparation Extern.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

Comparison with the paper

We found no statistical tests in the paper to compare with the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 2 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 01 Data Preparation Extern.R — numeric
2 Supplement_SG_v2.R — numeric

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

a script hit a could not find function "..." error; we added the library() calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
01 Data Preparation Extern.R ran_ok 4.2
Supplement_SG_v2.R errored undefined_variable 2.5

Undefined-variable errors

1 script failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

File Missing variable Defined in
Supplement_SG_v2.R kable_styling (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)

setwd() in the code

1 script calls setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): 01 Data Preparation Extern.R.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
01 Data Preparation Extern.R 2 (non-literal)

library() calls added

1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself. The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the library() calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after adding library() calls it should make itself.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

After registration, participants were directed to the baseline survey (T1) which included questions about trait-level personal characteristics (e.g., neuroticism, depression).

After receiving a prompt, participants had 60 minutes to complete the survey.

Every night (at 9pm), participants were invited to a daily-diary assessment.

Participants had 180 minutes to respond to this prompt.

Furthermore, participants completed a checklist of major life stressors, provided information on the timing of all experienced events, and identified the most important major life stressor they had experienced in the last month (i.e., since the start of the study).

We preregistered to exclude data from these assessments if participants completed a survey in less than 1 minute and additionally responded to more than 80% of the items for personality traits, reassurance seeking, depression, and rumination with the same response; however, no participant had to be excluded based on this criterion.

On average, participants completed 44.46 ESM surveys (nobservations = 18,360) and 9.61 daily dairies (nobservations = 3,727).

Participants were on average 26.86 years old (SD = 8.99); 69% of the sample were female and 93% of the sample reported having at least a high school diploma.

Participants were primarily German (55%) or Swiss (27%).

Ethics approval statement:

Data collection of the Stress and Personality Assessment (SPA) Study was approved by local ethics committee of University of Zurich [Protocol number: 24.08.22] and data were collected in accordance with the 2024 version of the Declaration of Helsinki.

description The SPA-Study will employ an experience sampling design, comprising two trait assessments and a 2-week experience sampling phase. The study will be addressed to the general public and data will be collected using formR UZH (https://formr-admin.psych.uzh.ch).
The overall goal of the SPA-Study will be to provide a better understanding of stress generation processes in daily life. Stress generation refers to the phenomenon that individuals actively contribute to the occurrence of stressful events in their lives (Hammen, 1991, 2006). Existing stress generation research has shown that personal characteristics like personality traits predict the occurrence of major life stressors several months or years later (Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023). However, less is known about the process of stress generation on shorter time scales in daily life, that is, how momentary personal characteristics predict the occurrence of minor stressors (also called daily hassles). Data from the SPA-Study will be used to examine how different momentary personal characteristics predict the occurrence of daily hassles and to explore possible mechanisms of these effects.
