How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Stress generation describes that people with mental health problems actively contribute to the occurrence of stressful events in their lives, which can lead to detrimental cycles between stress and mental health. However, existing research has focused on long-term stress generation. Here, we aimed to advance the understanding of how stress generation unfolds across different timescales by combing experience sampling, daily diary, and 1-month longitudinal data (N = 403). We found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism were linked to the occurrence of daily hassles over hours and days and major life stressors over a month. Furthermore, momentary neuroticism and rumination prospectively predicted the occurrence of daily hassles over several hours. Finally, some indicators of hourly and daily stress generation prospectively predicted the occurrence of major life stressors. These findings provide the starting point for a thorough understanding of how stress generation unfolds over time.

Stress Generation Across Hours, Days, and One Month

Stressful events, such as relationship conflicts, job loss, or divorce, have been linked to a broad range of detrimental outcomes, including the onset of mental disorders, physical health problems, and decreases in well-being (Asselmann et al., 2017; Cohen et al., 2019; DeLongis et al., 1982; Haehner, Fliedner, et al., 2024; Luhmann et al., 2012). Given that stress is related to both negative subclinical outcomes and risk for mental health diagnoses, it is crucial to understand when, why, and to whom such stressful events occur. Existing research shows that personal characteristics like neuroticism, depression, reassurance seeking, and rumination prospectively predict the occurrence of stressful events (R. T. Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023).

Stress generation refers to processes by which people actively contribute to the occurrence of stressful events in their lives (Hammen, 1991). For example, individuals with high levels of neuroticism are more likely to experience a job loss or a friendship dissolution (Beck & Jackson, 2022; Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024), in part because their behaviors elicit negative reactions in others.

Although there is robust evidence for the general phenomenon of stress generation, little is known about how stress generation processes unfold across different time intervals (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026). The majority of existing research has focused on stress generation over several weeks, months, or years (Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023), often neglecting stress generation processes at shorter timescales like hours or days (Cummings et al., 2010; Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Sahl et al., 2009). A thorough examination of how stress generation unfolds across different time intervals is needed for several reasons. First, relevant stress generation processes may be overlooked by focusing on long-term stress generation (i.e., months or years).

For example, rumination may predict the occurrence of stressful events over hours or days but not over weeks nor months (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; Starr et al., 2025). The limited attention that current stress generation theories give to the timescale of stress generation processes highlights the importance of empirical research on this topic to guide theory development (Hammen, 2006; Harkness & Washburn, 2016; R. T. Liu, 2013). Second, investigating stress generation across multiple time intervals enables an examination of how shorter-and longer-term stress generation may influence each other over time, helping to uncover potential mechanisms across timescales. Third, knowledge on how stress generation processes unfold across different time intervals is needed to design optimal assessment schedules in future research and identify ideal time points for interventions (Haehner, Wright, et al., 2026; Hopwood et al., 2022).

With the present study, we aimed to better understand how stress generation processes unfold across different timescales. Using data from the Stress and Personality Assessment (SPA) Study, which combined experience sampling, daily diary, and longitudinal survey methods, we examined stress generation processes over hours, days, and one month. We also explored whether stress generation processes across shorter time intervals predicted stress generation effects observed at longer time intervals.

Long-Term Stress Generation

Stress generation research seeks to explain why people differ in the exposure of stressful events. Stressful events describe time-discrete life experiences that disrupt people's life and that require adjustment by the individual (Wheaton et al., 2013). Stressful events differ in their intensity and frequency, including both daily hassles-minor, frequently occurring events that lead to short-term disruptions in daily life such as relationship conflicts-and major life stressors-rare disruptions that lead to lasting changes in people's lives like job loss or divorce (Haehner, Fliedner, et al., 2024; Kanner et al., 1981; Monroe, 1983). Hammen (1991) developed the Stress Generation Hypothesis to explain the observation that depressed individuals experience more dependent stressful events than non-depressed individuals. Dependent stressful events are those events that at least partly depend on the behavior of a person (e.g., a relationship breakup). In contrast, independent stressful events (e.g., death of a loved one) are theorized to be relatively independent of a person's influence.

The Stress Generation Hypothesis posits that depressed people behave in a way that leads to the occurrence of dependent but not independent stressful events.

The Stress Generation Hypothesis has received strong empirical support since its inception and its propositions have further been expanded to other constructs beyond depression (Hammen, 2006; R. T. Liu et al., 2024; R. T. Liu & Alloy, 2010). In two recent meta-analyses, Rnic et al. (2023) and Santee et al. (2023) found that different kinds of psychopathology and broader psychological risk factors predict the occurrence of major life stressors in clinical and non-clinical populations. Specifically, internalizing risk factors such as depression (r = .24), rumination (r = .26), reassurance seeking, (r = .17), and neuroticism (r = .17) have consistently been linked to the occurrence of dependent major life stressors in prospective longitudinal studies. These meta-analyses, however, also found small associations between these risk factors and the occurrence of independent major life stressors, suggesting that there may be processes leading to person-stressor links beyond stress generation such as reporting biases (e.g., people with higher levels of neuroticism may be more likely to report the occurrence of any kind of stressful events). Importantly, the existing evidence also shows that stress generation could be a mechanism contributing to the chronicity of mental health symptoms. Rnic et al. (2023), for example, found that stress generation could lead to a vicious cycle, with mental health symptoms predicting the occurrence of major life stressors, which in turn predicted an increase of mental health symptoms over time.

In sum, there is convincing evidence that personal characteristics like depression or neuroticism predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events in clinical and non-clinical populations. However, existing research primarily focused on longer-term stress generation processes over weeks (Hasegawa et al., 2023; Judah et al., 2013; Potthoff et al., 1995; Shih, 2006), months (Cox et al., 2009; Howe et al., 2017), or years (Conway et al., 2018; Goldstein et al., 2021). In contrast, stress generation processes over shorter time intervals (e.g., hours, days) that focus on daily hassles as outcomes have received comparatively less attention.

Short-Term Stress Generation

Short-term stress generation refers to the links between momentary, state-level personal characteristics and the occurrence of dependent daily hassles over several hours or days (e.g., Cummings et al., 2010; Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Sears et al., 2018). State-level personal characteristics describe momentary thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that are brief expressions of an individual's stable traits and probabilistically linked to their trait levels (Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2015; Rauthmann et al., 2015). For example, although people vary in how much they ruminate during any given moment in time, a person with a higher trait level of rumination is more likely to express state-level instances of rumination, such as ruminating about their romantic relationship.

Research on short-term stress generation complements findings on longer-term stress generation in three ways. First, rather than focusing on relatively infrequent major life stressors, short-term stress generation examines daily hassles as outcomes of stress generation processes. Daily hassles such as relationship conflicts are important outcomes of stress generation processes, because the accumulation of daily hassles has been found to be of similar relevance for health and well-being as the occurrence of major life stressors (Cohen et al., 2019; Kanner et al., 1981; Monroe, 1983). Second, studies on short-term stress generation typically focus on within-person instead of between-person effects (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; Sahl et al., 2009). For example, long-term stress generation research has examined whether individuals with higher or lower trait-levels of depression experience greater or fewer major life stressors (i.e., a between-person effect), whereas short-term stress generation research instead examines whether higher momentary levels of depression than usual predict the subsequent occurrence of daily hassles (i.e., a within-person effect). Knowledge on these within-person effects is crucial to develop effective interventions against stress generation (e.g., by selecting relevant intervention strategies that target problematic states) and can help to understand the mechanisms underlying between-person differences (Haehner, Wright, et al., 2026; Hopwood et al., 2025). Third, intensive longitudinal data collections such as experience sampling or dailydiary studies are used to examine short-term stress generation processes (Starr et al., 2025).

Studies with these designs can investigate risk factors of stress generation and daily hassles with a high temporal resolution and thus reduce risks of memory and recall bias (Conway et al., 2024; Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Shih & Auerbach, 2010).

Initial evidence supports the existence of short-term stress generation processes. For example, Sahl et al. (2009) showed in a 1-week daily-diary study that higher than usual hostile but not sad mood in the morning prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles reported in the evening. Similarly, Eberhart and Hammen (2009) found that higher levels of reassurance seeking and anxious attachment compared to one's personal average predicted the occurrence of relationship conflicts during the same day. Furthermore, Conway et al. (2024) showed that negative urgency prospectively predicted the occurrence of interpersonal daily hassles over several hours. In contrast, Vize et al. (2024) did not find a predictive effect of negative affect on the occurrence of daily hassles at the next assessment.

Finally, there is meta-analytic evidence that between-person differences in levels of depression (r = .13) and neuroticism (r = .10) prospectively predict the occurrence of daily hassles over several days (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026).

There are, however, several limitations of existing research on short-term stress generation that impede a comprehensive understanding of the temporal unfolding of these processes. First, most studies did not examine whether state-level personal characteristics prospectively predict the occurrence of dependent daily hassles, providing limited insight into the temporal direction of person-hassle transactions (Cummings et al., 2010; Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Shih & Auerbach, 2010; but see Conway et al., 2024). Second, only a few studies moved beyond daily assessment intervals (i.e., incorporated multiple assessments per day), so the question of whether stress generation unfolds across even shorter timescales still needs to be addressed (but see Conway et al., 2024; Sears et al., 2018; Vize et al., 2024). Third, existing research has not yet compared stress generation processes across different timescales, thereby providing little insight into how stress generation effects may diverge or converge across time intervals. Thus, the first goal of the present study was to examine whether established predictors of stress generation-depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism-predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events over hours, days, and one month.

Stress Generation Across Timescales

Examining stress generation across different timescales also enables an examination of how short-and long-term stress generation processes are related to each other. In line with theories on person-environment transactions, Haehner, Andrae, et al. (2026) hypothesized that short-term stress generation processes are the building blocks of long-term stress generation.

For example, behaving more neurotic than usual in a given moment may lead to the experience of a dependent daily hassle like a relationship conflict. Over time, these within-person effects may accumulate and explain the between-person and long-term longitudinal link between trait neuroticism and dependent major life stressors (e.g., ongoing relationship conflicts causing a breakup).

However, this hypothesis has not yet been empirically tested and other researchers have posited that the generation of dependent daily hassles and dependent major life stressors may be relatively independent of each other. For instance, Starr et al. (2025) suggested that although "hassle generation" may be a clinically relevant form of stress generation in its own regard, it may not necessarily be related to the generation of major life stressors, because many hassles that are stressful in the short-term result in desirable outcomes in the long run (e.g., dealing with relationship conflicts could even lead to a more resilient relationship). To evaluate these conflicting views, a second goal of the present study was to examine whether stress generation over hours or days predicts stress generation processes occurring over one month.

The Present Study

The goal of the present study was to better understand the temporal unfolding of stress generation processes. We examined links between four established risk factors of stress generation-depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism-and the occurrence of dependent stressful events across three timescales: hours using experience sampling data, days using daily-diary data, and one month using longitudinal surveys. The hourly and daily timescales captured short-term stress generation processes with daily hassles as the dependent variable whereas the monthly timescale was used to capture longer-term stress generation processes with major life stressors as the dependent variable. We addressed two research questions: (1) Which personal characteristics predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events across hours, days, and one month? (2) Do stress generation processes over hours and days predict stress generation over the course of one month? Furthermore, we also explored these same research questions for independent stressful events to probe the distinction between dependent and independent events emphasized by the Stress Generation Hypothesis.

Based on existing evidence on short-and long-term stress generation, we tested six confirmatory hypotheses: Depression and neuroticism predict the occurrence of dependent daily hassles over days (Hypotheses 1 and 2), and depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism predict the occurrence of major life stressors over one month (Hypotheses 3 to 6).

Transparency and Openness

Preregistration

Data collection was preregistered at https://osf.io/mfjc8/overview?view_only=8f2419af4907402cb05d623158cbd462. Hypotheses and the analysis plan were preregistered at https://osf.io/cg98k/overview?view_only=c759a5d3eb5c45f683418b20cf58f312. Deviations from the preregistration are summarized in the Supplementary Materials.

Data, Materials, Code, and Online Resources

Data, a codebook (including a list of all items), analysis scripts, and Supplementary Materials can be retrieved from https://osf.io/pcjnb/overview?view_only=52f63069dc1849f1b53c37b813a92e03. Data analysis was conducted in R (Version 4.5.3) using packages lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017), glmmTB (Brooks et al., 2017), and marginaleffects (Arel-Bundock, 2021). Some robustness checks were conducted in MPlus (Version 8.11; Muthén & Muthén, 2024).

Reporting

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study. A detailed list of all measures can be found in the https://osf.io/mfjc8/overview?view_only=8f2419af4907402cb05d623158cbd462.

Ethical Approval

Data collection of the Stress and Personality Assessment (SPA) Study was approved by local ethics committee of University of Zurich [Protocol number: 24.08.22] and data were collected in accordance with the 2024 version of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Methods

Procedure

The SPA Study consisted of two survey assessments one month apart with a 2-week experience sampling phase in between. Data were collected using formR (Arslan et al., 2020).

Participants interested in the SPA Study first had to complete a registration form and provide informed consent. After registration, participants were directed to the baseline survey (T1) which included questions about trait-level personal characteristics (e.g., neuroticism, depression).

Furthermore, participants could pick an individual start date for the experience sampling phase within 2 weeks after the baseline assessment.

During the 2-week experience sampling phase, participants received email invitations for six experience sampling method (ESM) surveys and one daily-diary survey per day. The ESM surveys were pseudo-randomly distributed throughout the day, with assessments being prompted during the following intervals: (1) 9am -9:45 am, (2) 11am -11:45 pm, (3) 1pm -1:45pm, (4) 3pm -3:45pm, (5) 5pm -5:45pm, (6) 7pm -7:45pm. After receiving a prompt, participants had 60 minutes to complete the survey. In the ESM surveys, participants rated their momentary personal characteristics (e.g., momentary rumination) and were asked whether they had experienced a daily hassle since the last assessment and, if yes, provided details on the event occurrence.

Every night (at 9pm), participants were invited to a daily-diary assessment. Participants had 180 minutes to respond to this prompt. In the daily-diary assessments, participants reported on their thoughts, feelings, and behaviors throughout the day. Furthermore, participants received a checklist of daily hassles, provided information on the timing of all experienced hassles, and identified the most important hassle of each day.

After the experience sampling phase, there was a break of up to 2 weeks-depending on participants' individualized start date. The post assessment (T2) then comprised questions about participants' trait-level personal characteristics, similar to the baseline assessment.

Furthermore, participants completed a checklist of major life stressors, provided information on the timing of all experienced events, and identified the most important major life stressor they had experienced in the last month (i.e., since the start of the study). More details about the study design can be found in the study design preregistration at https://hmupm-my.sharepoint.com/personal/peter_haehner_hmu-duesseldorf-krefeld_de/Documents/Professur%20HMU/Forschungsprojekte/31%20Stress%20Generation%20Across%20Timescales/Revision/ore%20details%20about%20the%20study%20design%20can%20be%20found%20in%20the%20study%20design%20preregistration%20at%20https:/osf.io/mfjc8/?view_only=8f2419af4907402cb05d623158cbd462.

Participants

The SPA Study included German speaking adults (minimum age: 18 years).

Recruitment addressed people who frequently feel stressed. Participants could receive up to CHF 30 for taking part in the study with compensation being contingent on the completion of the surveys. Furthermore, participants could receive partial course credit and feedback on their Big Five personality trait profile.

Overall, 591 people registered to take part in the SPA Study. However, for the present study, only participants who started the phase of intensive longitudinal assessments were considered (n = 414). Furthermore, we excluded data from the baseline and post assessments (n = 11) if a participant failed to respond correctly to one or more instructed response items (e.g., "To ensure data quality, please select the response option 3"). Additionally, for the ESM and daily-diary assessments, we checked for careless responding using the longstring indicator from the careless package (Yentes & Wilhelm, 2023). We preregistered to exclude data from these assessments if participants completed a survey in less than 1 minute and additionally responded to more than 80% of the items for personality traits, reassurance seeking, depression, and rumination with the same response; however, no participant had to be excluded based on this criterion.

Applying these exclusion criteria led to a final sample size of N = 403. On average, participants completed 44.46 ESM surveys (nobservations = 18,360) and 9.61 daily dairies (nobservations = 3,727). Participants were on average 26.86 years old (SD = 8.99); 69% of the sample were female and 93% of the sample reported having at least a high school diploma.

Participants were primarily German (55%) or Swiss (27%). More details on the sample can be found in Section 1 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f. Power simulations indicated that we had sufficient power (1 -β ≥ .80) to identify small stress generation effects across all three timescales (hours: β = 0.05; days: β = 0.12; weeks: β = 0.08) and medium-sized interaction effects across timescales (β = 0.23).

Measures

Stressful Events

At the hourly timescale (ESM assessments), participants indicated whether they had experienced a daily hassle since the last assessment ("Have you experienced a negative or stressful event since the last assessment?" ;0 = no,1 = yes) and described the hassle in an openresponse field (M = 11.06 words, SD = 14.58 words). We coded these free-text responses to determine the stressfulness (0 = no,1 = maybe,2 = yes) and the dependence of the reported events (0 = independent,1 = unclear,2 = dependent), with detailed definitions of these coding categories provided in the https://osf.io/q2693?view_only=52f63069dc1849f1b53c37b813a92e03 for details). Interrater agreement was good (κ = .86 to .93) and divergent ratings were resolved by the decision of an independent coder. We used these ratings to create two binary variables: dependent hassle occurrence (0 = no dependent hassle since the last assessment,1 = dependent hassle experienced since the last assessment) and independent event occurrence (0 = no independent hassle since the last assessment,1 = independent hassle experienced since the last assessment).

At the daily timescale (daily-diary assessments), participants received a checklist of daily hassles and checked all events they had experienced on that day. This checklist was based on existing approaches (Cummings et al., 2010; Sahl et al., 2009) and we categorized hassles as dependent (failed to reach a personal goal at work, university or school; received negative feedback on my performance at work, university or school; failed to reach a daily fitness goal; did something embarrassing in a social situation; argument or conflict with partner or family members; argument or conflict with friend or other close person; argument or conflict with a stranger; been hurt, rejected or criticized by a close person) or independent (illness or injury; mobility-related problem; victim of crime; technical problems). For the analyses, we created sum scores of experienced dependent and independent hassles at the respective day.

At the monthly timescale (post assessment), participants received a checklist of major life stressors and were asked to check all events they had experienced in the past month (i.e., since the start of the study). This checklist was based on existing approaches (Hankin et al., 2010; Hasegawa et al., 2023) and we categorized events as either dependent (job loss; end of a relationship; divorce; end of friendship; serious conflicts in the family; serious conflicts in the partnership; serious conflicts with friends or other close people; serious professional conflicts; failed to pass an important exam; dropping out of studies; training or other further education, problems with the police or a legal dispute) or independent (death of a loved one; injury or illness of a loved one; own illness or injury; miscarriage). For the analyses, we created sum scores of experienced dependent and independent major life stressors.

Depression

Depression was assessed with the German version of the Patient Health Questionnaire (Kroenke et al., 2001; Kuczynski et al., 2022; Löwe et al., 2005). Items (e.g., "I felt down, depressed, or hopeless" or "I had little interest or pleasure in doing things") were assessed on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 7 (completely). Items were presented with different timeframes in the instructions at the three timescales (i.e., since the last assessment, today, in the last month). We used eight items at the monthly timescale and two items at the hourly and daily timescale (monthly: α = .85; daily: rinter-item = .69; hourly: rinter-item = .64).

Rumination

Rumination was assessed with the German version of the Experience Sampling

Rumination Measure (Hoebeke et al., 2022). Items (e.g., "I was thinking about emotional experiences" or "I was thinking about the causes and consequences of emotional experiences") were rated on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very often). Items were presented with different timeframes in the instructions at the three timescales (i.e., since the last assessment, today, in the last month). We used five items across all timescales (monthly: α = .82; daily: rinter-item = .58, ωbetween = .88, ωwithin = .79; hourly: rinter-item = .58; ωbetween = .89, ωwithin = .78).

Reassurance Seeking

Reassurance seeking was assessed using the German version of the Reassurance Seeking Scale (Meyer et al., 2023; Rector et al., 2011). Items (e.g., "How many times did you seek reassurance before making a decision?" or "How many times did you seek reassurance that everything is alright?") were rated on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very often). Items were presented with different timeframes in the instructions at the three timescales (i.e., since the last assessment, today, in the last month). We used nine items for the monthly timescale and three items for the hourly and daily timescale (monthly: α = .85; daily: rinter-item = .58, ωbetween = .92, ωwithin = .63; hourly: rinter-item = .52; ωbetween = .94, ωwithin = .60). Furthermore, at the hourly timescale, reassurance seeking was only assessed when participants indicated that they had interacted with another person since the last assessment.

Neuroticism

Neuroticism was assessed with bipolar adjective scales (e.g., tense vs. relaxed or clam vs. irritable), based on Bleidorn et al. (2009) and Ringwald et al. (2022). Items were presented with different timeframes in the instructions at the three timescales (i.e., since the last assessment, today, in the last month). We used two items at the monthly timescale and one item for the hourly and daily timescales (monthly: α = .75).

Data Analysis

We used a level of significance of α = .05 for the present analyses. To facilitate the interpretation of effects, we standardized all personal characteristics using their grand mean and grand standard deviation at their respective timescale. For example, we standardized ESM depression using the mean and standard deviation of all ESM depression ratings. Using this approach, all effects have a comparable metric across constructs and timescales (i.e., timescale specific standard deviation units).

Research Question 1: Which Variables Predict the Occurrence of Dependent Stressful Events Across Hours, Days, or Weeks?

To examine hourly stress generation, we used logistic multilevel models with assessments (j) nested in participants (i). The occurrence of dependent daily hassles since the last assessment served as binary dependent variable (0 = no,1 = yes). The person-mean of a personal characteristic (e.g., person-mean of depression) and the person-mean centered personal characteristic at the previous assessment (e.g., person-mean centered depression at j -1) served as predictors to examine between-person effects and lagged within-person effects, respectively. Furthermore, we controlled for the time interval between assessments (standardized), whether assessments occurred on weekends versus weekdays, and gender (dichotomized). An example model equation reads as follows: We used a similar analysis strategy to examine daily stress generation. The main difference was that we used the number of experienced dependent daily hassles on a certain day as dependent variable as opposed to the binary hassle indicator. Consequently, we used Poisson multilevel models instead of logistic multilevel models to model this count variable. To increase interpretability of effects, we transformed fixed effects to incidence rate ratios (IRR) and count differences (CD). CD describe the absolute difference in the number of expected events between people with different levels of the predictor (e.g., +1 SD vs. -1 SD of depressive symptoms).

Finally, to examine monthly stress generation, we moved from a multilevel modeling framework to single-level Poisson regression models. In these models, we did not distinguish between-person and within-person effects (as is typical in long-term stress generation research), but we used the personal characteristics assessed at baseline as predictors of the number of dependent major life stressors reported at post assessment, thus establishing temporal precedence of the predictors. We again included gender and time (but not weekday) as covariates and transformed effects to IRR and CD to increase interpretability.

Research Question 2: Do Stress Generation Processes on Shorter Timescales Explain

Stress Generation Processes on Longer Timescales?

For Research Question 2, we were interested in whether and how stress generation processes across different timescales interacted with each other. We examined two processes predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors across the study period.

The interaction effects (b5, b6, and b7) indicate whether monthly stress generation effects (i.e., the association between the baseline personal characteristic and the number of dependent major life stressors) depended on aggregated characteristics of the hourly stress generation processes.

A significant positive interaction effect would indicate that stress generation processes in daily life amplify long-term stress generation effects. To increase interpretability, we again transformed coefficients to IRR.

To examine the interplay of daily and monthly stress generation, we repeated these analyses using data assessed in the daily diaries and random effects from the stress-generationover-days model. We again examined main effects and the interaction effects of the daily stress generation indicators to evaluate the interplay of daily and monthly stress generation effects.

Exploratory Analysis

To examine the specificity of stress generation effects for dependent stressful events, we repeated all analyses using independent stressful events as criterion variables. This allowed us to compare effect sizes for the generation of dependent and independent stressful events and thus provided a more stringent test of the Stress Generation Hypothesis (Hammen, 1991).

Results

Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive statistics for all study variables across the three timescales are summarized in Table 1. Overall, participants reported relatively few dependent stressful events across the study period, with dependent daily hassles reported at 5% of assessments in the ESM surveys (ntotal = 992), an average of 0.49 dependent daily hassles in the daily diaries (ntotal = 1,829), and an average of 0.36 dependent major life stressors in the post assessment (ntotal = 145). The different predictors of stress generation showed small to medium within-person correlations (hourly:.01 ≤ r ≤ .40, daily:.06 ≤ r ≤ .41) and medium to strong between-person correlations (hourly:.08 ≤ r ≤ .70, daily:.21 ≤ r ≤ .69, monthly:.25 ≤ r ≤ .57). Further descriptive statistics can be found in Section 1 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f. Note. The hourly timescale refers to the ESM assessments, the daily timescale to the daily diaries, and the monthly timescale to the baseline and the post assessment. At the hourly timescale, participants received questions about reassurance seeking only when they indicated that they had interacted with someone since the last assessment explaining the lower sample size for this variable. Dependent and independent stressful events were assessed as metric variables at the daily and the monthly timescale but as binary variables at the hourly timescale. Thus, the mean for the hourly timescale can be interpreted as the proportion of assessments at which a stressful event occurred. At the monthly level, stressful events refer to major life stressors whereas at the hourly and daily level stressful events refer to daily hassles. Further descriptive statistics including distributions can be found in Section 1 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f. ICC = intra-class correlation.

Research Question 1: Which Variables Predict the Occurrence of Dependent Stressful

Events Across Hours, Days, or Weeks?

As a first step, we examined whether depressive symptoms, rumination, reassurance seeking, and depression predicted the occurrence of dependent stressful events across hours, days, and one month. The results of these analyses are illustrated in Figure 1 and summarized in Table 2. Overall, we found robust evidence for between-person effects across all timescales.

That is, higher average levels of depressive symptoms, neuroticism, reassurance seeking, and rumination consistently predicted the occurrence of a higher number of dependent stressful events. Effect sizes ranged from OR = 1.28 to OR = 1.74 across hours, from IRR = 1.28 to IRR = 1.58 across days, and from IRR = 1.19 to IRR = 1.34 across one month, indicating small between-person associations (Chen et al., 2010; Funder & Ozer, 2019). In other words, a person with above average levels (+ 1 SD) of depressive symptoms, neuroticism, reassurance seeking, and rumination has a 0.02 to 0.03 point higher probability to experience a hassle at the hourly timescale, experiences 0.12 to 0.25 more hassles more at the daily timescale, and 0.08 to 0.14 more hassles at the monthly timescale than a person with average levels.

Evidence for within-person effects was less consistent. Within-person increases in rumination (OR = 1.16) and neuroticism (OR = 1.19) prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles at the hourly timescale, but no other within-person effect reached statistical significance. Thus, our findings were in line with Hypotheses 3 to 6 (depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism predict dependent stressful events over one month) and partly in line with Hypotheses 1 and 2 (depression and neuroticism predict stressful events over days) as we only found significant between-person effects.

As people reported relatively few dependent stressful events across the study period, we repeated the analyses of the daily and monthly stress generation model, using logistic instead of Poisson regressions by dichotomizing the dependent variable (0 = no dependent stressful experienced,1 = at least one dependent stressful event experienced). All significant effects from our main analysis replicated in this robustness check, supporting the robustness of findings across the two analysis approaches (see Section 2 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f for details). Stress Generation Effects over Hours, Days, and One Month Note. This figure depicts between-person (upper panel) and within-person (lower panel) effects for stress generation across hours, days, and one month. No within-person effects could be estimated at the monthly level.

For the hourly timescale, odds ratios are predicted. For the daily and monthly timescale, incidence risk ratios are shown. Significant effects (p < .05) are depicted with circles.

Research Question 2: Do Stress Generation Processes on Shorter Timescales Predict

Stress Generation Processes on Longer Timescales?

In a second step, we examined whether stress generation processes observed at shorter timescales could predict stress generation processes on longer timescales. The findings from these analyses are illustrated in Figures 2 and 3.

Adding indicators from the hourly stress generation model to the monthly model, we found that a higher number of dependent daily hassles at the hourly level predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment in two of the four models (reassurance seeking: IRR = 1.29, p = .004; neuroticism: IRR = 1.27, p = .042). These findings indicate that people who experience more dependent hassles at the hourly timescale also tend to report a higher number of major life stressors at post assessment. Furthermore, higher average ratings of depressive symptoms (IRR = 1.78, p = .001) and rumination (IRR = 1.39, p = .011) during the ESM surveys predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment, suggesting that these average momentary ratings of depression and rumination predict the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment beyond people's baseline levels of these traits. Finally, there was only one interaction effect between indicators of hourly stress generation and people's baseline characteristics and this effect was in an unexpected direction. People who reported a higher number of dependent hassles in the ESM surveys had weaker links between reassurance seeking at baseline and the occurrence of dependent major life stressors (IRR = 0.67, p = .001).

Two of these effects were replicated when adding indicators from the daily stress generation model to the monthly model. Specifically, higher levels of depressive symptoms (IRR = 1.60, p = .003) and rumination (IRR = 1.38, p = .031) during the daily diaries predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment, supporting that momentary ratings of these constructs have predictive value for the occurrence of major life stressors above and beyond people's baseline levels of these traits. Furthermore, we found a positive interaction between people's baseline levels of neuroticism and the number of reported dependent hassles on dependent major life stressors (IRR = 1.54, p = .048). This effect indicates that people who experience more daily hassles have stronger links between their baseline neuroticism and the number of reported dependent major life stressors. However, the findings from these crosstimescale analyses should be interpreted with caution because we found that the person-specific slopes (SGhours and SGdays) that we extracted from the hourly and daily stress generation models had a low reliability (hourly: .05 to .49; daily: .58 to .60). Thus, the lack of cross-timescale interactions may at least partly be explained by the limited precession to capture these effects in our sample. Exploratory Analysis: Independent Events

In a final preregistered step, we repeated all analyses using independent instead of dependent stressful events as the criterion variable. The results of these analyses are summarized in Table 3. Similar to the results for dependent stressful events, between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism predicted the occurrence of independent hassles over hours and days. However, only one effect emerged at the monthly timescale, only the within-person stress generation effect for ESM neuroticism replicated, whereas the within-person effect for rumination was in the opposite direction, and effect sizes tended to be slightly smaller than for dependent events (hours:1.24 ≤ OR ≤ 1.68,0.010 ≤ RD ≤ 0.023; days:1.24 ≤ IRR ≤ 1.44,0.052 ≤ CD ≤ 0.096; month:1.05 ≤ IRR ≤ 1.34,0.009 ≤ CD ≤ 0.055). Furthermore, there was only one significant effect in models that combined short-and long-term predictors of independent major life stressors (see Section 3 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f for details). The only exception was that a higher number of independent stressful events in the ESM surveys was linked to a higher number of independent major life stressors at post assessment in the neuroticism model (IRR = 1.40, p = .029).
