Discussion

With the present study, we aimed to advance our understanding of how stress generation unfolds across different timescales. Using hourly, daily, and monthly data, we found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism were robustly linked to the occurrence of dependent stressful events across all three timescales.

A person with above average levels of depressive symptoms, neuroticism, reassurance seeking, and rumination has a 0.02 to 0.03 point higher probability to experience a hassle at the hourly timescale, experiences 0.12 to 0.25 more hassles more at the daily timescale, and 0.08 to 0.14 more hassles at the monthly timescale. Furthermore, within-person increases in neuroticism and rumination prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles at the next assessment, providing insights into the mechanisms of stress generation in daily life. Crosstimescale analyses showed that the occurrence of dependent daily hassles and average momentary depression and rumination ratings predicted the occurrence of major life stressors over one month, illustrating their utility to predict long-term stress generation effects above and beyond baseline levels of these traits. In contrast, we found limited evidence for interactions of stress generation processes across timescales, which could partly be explained by methodological problems to capture these interactions, outlining the necessity for future crosstemporal research. In the following, we discuss the insights of our study for short-term stress generation and the interplay of stress generation process across timescales.

Short-Term Stress Generation Processes

Stress generation research has traditionally focused on longer-term longitudinal links between personal characteristics and the occurrence of dependent major life stressors over several weeks, months, or years (Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023). In line with the existing evidence on this topic, we found that people with higher levels of depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism reported a higher number of dependent major life stressors a month later. Moving beyond the monthly level, we replicated these between-person associations at hourly and daily timescales. These effects indicate that people with higher average levels of depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism in daily life experience more dependent daily hassles than people with lower average levels of these risk factors. These results confirm and extend the initial evidence on stress generation, showing that depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism are important risk factors for the occurrence of dependent daily hassles and major life stressors across different timescales (Cummings et al., 2010; Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; Sahl et al., 2009; Shih & Auerbach, 2010).

Interestingly, between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism predicted both dependent and independent stressful events. Relatedly, correlations between personal characteristics and daily hassles were of similar size for dependent versus independent events (see Section 1 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f). These results are at odds with the Stress Generation Hypothesis but matches existing meta-analytic findings (Hammen, 1991; R. T. Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023). The Stress Generation Hypothesis states that people with certain risk factors should only differ in the experience of dependent stressful events, because they behave in a way that makes those events more likely. In contrast, independent stressful events are, by definition, out of a person's control. One explanation for why predictive effects for independent events may have emerged is reporting bias (Hammen, 2006; Monroe, 2008). People with higher levels of depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism may experience events as more stressful and thus be more likely to report these events as hassles (Haehner et al., 2023; Wenzel et al., 2025).

Designs that can separate the occurrence and the appraisal of events would be necessary to test this explanation (see Limitations section for details). An alternative explanation is that the dichotomous distinction between dependent and independent stressful events is imperfect.

Almost no event is entirely independent of the person (Kandler et al., 2012; Plomin & Bergeman, 1991). For example, technical and mobility-related problems were classified as independent daily hassles in the present study. However, one can easily imagine scenarios where these events actually depend on the behavior of a person (e.g., a computer crash because a person forgot to update their computer). An important direction for future research would thus be to move beyond the simplistic distinction of dependent and independent events and instead consider a broader range of relevant event characteristics that may help to understand which kinds of events people experience in which contexts (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; Starr et al., 2025).

We also examined whether state-level personal characteristics prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles (i.e., a prospective within-person effect). We found two within-person effects at the hourly timescale: Higher momentary levels of neuroticism and rumination relative to one's average predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles over several hours. These effects could indicate that being neurotic or ruminating in a given moment binds people's resources, which in turn could make the occurrence of dependent hassles like failing at a work-related task or being late to a meeting more likely. In line with the Stress Generation Hypothesis, these within-person effects were more consistent for dependent than for independent daily hassles. These results are similar to those reported by Sahl et al. (2009) and Conway et al. (2024) who found that hostility and a sense of urgency prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles. Together, these findings on within-person predictors of dependent daily hassles could provide initial insights into stress generation from a mechanistic perspective by drawing attention to how individuals generate stress (Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026). However, experimental approaches would be needed that manipulate state-level predictors of stress generation (e.g., temporary increase or decrease rumination) to fully understand stress generation mechanisms and to test the causal relevance of the identified within-person effects.

In summary, the present study shows that between-person associations among depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism with dependent daily hassles and major life stressors can be observed over hours, days, and one month. However, these effects may partly be inflated due to reporting bias or ambiguous distinctions between event types as we found similar associations for independent events. At the within-person level, being neurotic or ruminating in a given moment prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles, providing initial insights into the mechanisms of stress generation in daily life.

Stress Generation Effects Across Timescales

In addition to examining stress generation over hours, days, and one month, the present study aimed to better understand whether and how stress generation processes interact across relatively independently of each other, meaning that the processes that lead to the generation of daily hassles differ from those that lead to the occurrence of major life stressors.

Overall, we found limited evidence for interactions between short-and long-term stress generation processes, rather supporting the view of Starr and colleagues. However, there are some caveats to this conclusion. First, there were some main effects of indicators of short-term stress generation predicting the occurrence of major life stressors at post assessment. For example, higher average levels of depression and rumination in the ESM surveys and daily diaries predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors above and beyond people's baseline levels of depression and rumination. Similarly, the occurrence of dependent hassles in daily life predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment. Thus, even if short-term stress generation processes do not modulate long-term stress generation effects, indicators of short-term stress generation still improved the prediction of who experienced dependent major life stressors. This finding could thus be of practical relevance to design interventions to reduce stress generation, because it suggests that momentary expressions of rumination and depression would be suitable intervention targets (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026). For example, just-in-time adaptive interventions that target high statelevels of depression and rumination could serve a double purpose by reducing short-term stress generation processes and helping reduce people's trait levels of depression and neuroticism over time (Nahum-Shani et al., 2015).

Second, our analyses showed that investigating stress generation effects across timescales is challenging. Even though we had a relatively large number of observations (Nobs = 18,360), the person-specific slopes extracted from the daily and hourly stress generation models had a low reliability. Thus, the limited evidence for interactions across timescales could at least partly be explained by a lack of precision to identify these effects. However, beyond increasing the number of observations, the precision of these within-person slopes also depends on factors that are hard to control such as the within-person variance of predictors (S. Liu et al., 2021). Methodological advancements that can account for measurement error in these personspecific may help addressing this problem in the future (Lai & Liu, 2026).

A critical goal for future research would also be to further disentangle which stress generation predictors operate at which timescale to develop an integrative theoretical model.

Ideally, we would have specific hypotheses on how between-person differences in stable risk factors are related to within-person increases in relevant states that then lead to the occurrence of daily hassles and major life stressors. For example, neuroticism may best be conceptualized as a predictor of long-term stress generation whereas specific behaviors (e.g., a flippant reaction, a clingy behavior) may be the active ingredients of short-term stress generation.

Different assessment methods could help to clearly distinguish these predictors (e.g., self-report versus behavioral observation). Furthermore, future research should investigate the types of daily hassles more thoroughly. In the present study, we considered the overall sum of experienced daily hassles and people's overall state-level-hassle links as predictors of major life stressors. However, it could be the case that interactions between short-and long-term stress generation are domain-specific. For example, the accumulation of relationship conflicts may predict the occurrence of interpersonal major life stressors but not work-related major life stressors. Overall, the present study should thus be seen as a starting point to better understand the interplay of stress generation processes across timescales, hopefully inspiring future research on this topic.

In summary, we found limited evidence that stress generation processes interact across timescales, but some indicators of short-term stress generation processes-in particular

Limitations

The present study has several limitations. First, our sample was highly educated, predominantly female, and recruited in German-speaking Western countries. As stress generation research has primarily been conducted in the United States (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023), the findings of the present study can help to understand whether stress generation processes generalize across different Western contexts.

However, it remains unclear whether findings generalize to individuals from other socioeconomic or cultural backgrounds (R. T. Liu et al., 2024).

Second, participants reported relatively few stressful event occurrences across the study period. Although the number of event occurrences seems to be comparable those reported in existing research (e.g., Almeida et al., 2023), larger effects for stress generation may be observed in clinical samples, which tend to experience stressful events more frequently (Rnic et al., 2023). However, in particular, for the monthly timescale, for which we assessed major life stressors, a low base rate can generally be expected.

Third, we examined stress generation over one month to represent long-term stress generation. Although a time interval of one month could be a reasonable starting point when aiming to connect short-and long-term perspectives on stress generation, one month rather represents the lower bound for examining stress generation, with existing research mostly using time intervals of several months or years (Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023). This issue points to a broader conceptual problem: The time interval between assessments is a continuous variable, thus every categorization of time intervals is a simplification (Voelkle et al., 2018).

Fourth, the measures to assess depression, rumination, and reassurance seeking slightly differed across timescales. For example, we used fewer items to assess constructs in the ESM surveys and daily diaries. Assessing constructs like depression or neuroticism with few items may limit reliability and content validity (Rammstedt & Beierlein, 2014), which in turn could restrict power to identify significant effects. On the other hand, the higher number of ESM surveys compared to daily diaries increased power at the hourly timescale, which could explain why we only found within-person effects for the hourly timescale.

Fifth, in the present study, we did not use interview methods to capture the occurrence of stressful events. Interview methods are advantageous to assess the occurrence of stressful events because they may help disentangle stressor occurrence and personal characteristics (Hammen, 2006; Harkness & Monroe, 2016; Monroe, 2008; Santee et al., 2023). However, due to their high burden for researchers and participants, interview methods are more difficult to be integrated in intensive longitudinal studies (Starr et al., 2025). The reliance on self-report measures across timescales to assess both stressor occurrence and personal characteristics may have inflated associations in our study. Future research using interview methods may also help to more accurately distinguish between independent and dependent events.

Sixth, when examining stress generation processes across timescales, we used a twostep approach using indicators of short-term stress generation from the hourly and daily multilevel models as predictors of major life stressors in separate regressions. While alternative approaches could not directly be applied to our research question (e.g., MSEMs), this two-step approach is limited by the low reliability of the extracted effects (S. Liu et al., 2021). Future research on stress generation across timescales is needed to better understand possible interactions between short-and long-term stress generation. Studies with an even larger number of observations per person and methodological advancements that can account for unreliability of the two-step approach may help to address this problem in the future.

Conclusion

Large-scale longitudinal studies and comprehensive meta-analyses have shown that personal characteristics predict the occurrence of dependent major life stressors over several months and years, while the links between personal characteristics and dependent daily hassles over the course of hours and days have received comparatively less research attention (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; R. T. Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023). Examining stress generation over hours, days, and one month, we found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism are linked to the occurrence of dependent stressful events over hours, days, and one month, indicating that similar individual differences contribute to the generation of dependent daily hassles and major life stressor across different timescales. Furthermore, being neurotic and ruminating in a given moment prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles over several hours, pointing to a potential mechanism of stress generation in daily life. Finally, some indicators of shortterm stress generation-averaged state-level characteristics and the occurrence of dependent daily hassles-predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors over one month.

These findings provide a useful foundation for a more thorough empirical investigation and theoretical integration of how stress generation unfolds over time.

To examine the interplay of hourly and monthly stress generation, we first obtained person-level slopes (i.e., empirical Bayes estimates) from the hourly stress generation models from Research Question 1. These person-specific slopes capture between-person differences in the link between momentary personal characteristics and the occurrence of dependent daily hassles (henceforward called SGHours). Then, we added SGHours, the person-mean of the personal characteristics assessed in the ESM surveys (Person.mean), and each person's average number of experienced dependent stressful events during the ESM period (Event.avg) to the monthly stress generation model from Research Question 1. Furthermore, we included interactions between the baseline personal characteristic (PersBaseline) and SGHours, Person.mean, and Event.avg. An example model equation reads as follows: 𝐸𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑃𝑜𝑠𝑡 𝑖 = 𝑏 0 + 𝑏 1 • 𝑃𝑒𝑟𝑠 𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒 𝑖 + 𝑏 2 • 𝑃𝑒𝑟𝑠. 𝑚𝑒𝑎𝑛 𝐻𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑠 𝑖 + 𝑏 3 • 𝑆𝐺 𝐻𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑠 𝑖 + 𝑏 4 • 𝐸𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡. 𝑎𝑣𝑔 𝐻𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑠 𝑖 + 𝑏 5 • 𝑃𝑒𝑟𝑠 𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒 𝑖 • 𝑃𝑒𝑟𝑠. 𝑚𝑒𝑎𝑛 𝐻𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑠 𝑖 + 𝑏 6 • 𝑃𝑒𝑟𝑠 𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒 𝑖 • 𝑆𝐺 𝐻𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑠 𝑖 + 𝑏 7 • 𝑃𝑒𝑟𝑠 𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒 𝑖 • 𝐸𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡. 𝑎𝑣𝑔 𝐻𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑠 𝑖 + 𝑏 8 • 𝐺𝑒𝑛𝑑𝑒𝑟 𝑖 + 𝑏 9 • 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒 𝑖 + 𝜀 𝑖 b1 to b9 describe the link between the different predictor variables and the number of dependent major life stressors at post assessment. Scholars have expressed conflicting views about the existence and relevance of such interaction effects. Drawing on theories on person-environment transactions, Haehner, Andrae, et al. (2026) posited that short-term stress generation processes are the building blocks of long-term stress generation effects, implying that indicators of short-term stress generation should be able to predict long-term stress generation effects. In contrast, Starr et al. (2025) posited that short-and long-term stress generation processes likely operate people's average levels of state-level characteristics and the occurrence of dependent daily hassles-predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors above and beyond people's baseline personal characteristics.

These findings are an important first step towards a more comprehensive understanding of how stress generation processes unfold across different timescales. Future research on this topic is warranted, because it connects established findings of between-person effects on stress generation to its within-person mechanisms. This evidence is crucial to design effective interventions against stress generation because it helps to identify people at risk for stress generation (i.e., between-person effects) while also elucidating when and how individuals generate stress (i.e., within-person effects).
